{"success": true, "name": "arc-rectangle-noise-cleanup", "description": "Use when ARC grids contain rectangles and scattered noise.", "tags": ["arc", "rectangles", "denoising", "object-restoration"], "related_skills": ["continual-arc-solving"], "content": "---
name: arc-rectangle-noise-cleanup
description: Use when ARC grids contain rectangles and scattered noise.
metadata:
  hermes:
    tags: [arc, rectangles, denoising, object-restoration]
    related_skills: [continual-arc-solving]
---

# Restore rectangular objects and remove noise

Use this workflow when ARC demonstrations show uniform rectangular color patches mixed with sparse outlier pixels, corrupted cells, or nearby non-object marks. The usual operation is to preserve or complete genuine rectangular patches and replace unrelated noise with the background. Confirm the structure from the current task's demos; do not assume every patch-looking group is an object.

## Establish the transformation from demos

- Compare each demo input/output cell-by-cell. Record changed cells, preserved regions, and unchanged lookalike structures.
- Identify background color, object colors, and noise/corruption colors by role in the examples, not by numeric convention or frequency alone.
- Distinguish two operations: (a) restore anomalous cells *inside* a demonstrated rectangle to its uniform object color; (b) clear isolated/outside noise to the background. Do not clear object holes or preserve outside speckles merely because they share an object color.
- Confirm whether rectangles are intact input objects, partially corrupted rectangles, or regions reconstructed by extending a marker pattern. Only infer extension when examples establish it.

## Segment candidate objects before editing

1. Locate contiguous same-color blocks and record each candidate's bounding box, dimensions, and interior consistency.
2. Test whether a candidate is a solid rectangle except for sparse overlaid cells. Verify its outline and neighbors; an interior anomalous marker can be corruption, but one aligned stray cell outside the box does not prove the box should expand. Derive bounds from the repeated rows/columns of the patch, not only from connected components of its dominant color: an overlaid 7/8/etc. cell may split or shrink the apparent component while still lying inside the intended rectangle.
3. Treat similarly colored but disconnected patches as separate candidates unless demos establish a relation that joins them. Distinct rectangles can have different sizes and colors; apply the demonstrated object-selection criterion, and do not assume every patch-like cluster qualifies.
4. Do not elevate every small cluster or aligned fragment to an object. Use demonstrations to determine minimum size/shape and whether tiny rectangles count. A lone pixel, short fragment, and recurring large patch may have different roles.
5. Determine exact edges from evidence. Avoid including adjacent background, nearby distinct-color objects, or isolated marks in the bounds.

## Apply conservatively

- Start with the input copied exactly. Fill only confirmed rectangles to their inferred object color, correcting interior anomalies/holes as supported.
- Clear only confirmed noise cells outside those objects to the demonstrated background.
- Preserve every cell outside the selected rectangles and noise set. Do not blanket-recolor every occurrence of an uncommon color.
- In a multi-color, multi-demo patch-cleanup task, rectangles of different colors and dimensions may all be valid objects, including small 2×2 patches and patches whose cells resemble the background palette in other tasks. Do not select by color alone: use the demos' rectangular geometry, and clear scattered marks outside the exact boxes.
- Exact bounds matter: an adjacent, aligned speckle must not enlarge a patch. When repeated submissions fail, re-audit each patch's last row/column and ensure no extension includes neighboring background; also verify any apparent edge/corner corruption is actually inside the patch bounds.
- If multiple object-selection or boundary hypotheses remain and produce materially different outputs, use a demo request when its likely information value justifies the cost. Avoid submission-by-guessing when wrong attempts are costly.

## Confirmed hollow-frame parity recoloring pattern

A demonstrated family of tasks contains many hollow rectangular frames with arbitrary frame colors and interior holes or stray colors. Preserve the frame outline and replace every cell strictly inside each qualifying outline with an output color determined by the frame's dimensions, not its border color or the original interior contents: frames with both dimensions odd (e.g. 3×3, 5×5, 7×7, and 7×3) have their interiors filled with 7; frames with both dimensions even (e.g. 4×4, 6×6, and 8×8) have their interiors filled with 2. This was consistent across five demos, multiple palettes/backgrounds, and varied frame colors, and was independently reinforced by an eight-demo instance containing numerous hollow frames of different colors and dimensions: 3×3 and 7×7 frames had interiors recolored to 7, while 4×4 frames had interiors recolored to 2. Leave frame borders, surrounding background, and unrelated regions unchanged. No mixed-parity frame (one even and one odd dimension) was demonstrated, so do not infer its output without additional evidence. For each candidate frame, measure the complete outline bounds first and calculate height/width from those bounds; the parity mapping uses the full outer frame dimensions (including border), not the interior dimensions. Restore the entire enclosed interior uniformly, including any original background-colored cells, sparse anomaly cells, or holes. Do not treat stray interior marks as border extensions.

When this specific regularity appears, don't apply the ordinary “fill with the frame color” cleanup rule: the interior output palette is the parity code (7/2), independent of frame color. Validate the parity classification of every frame individually before submitting.

Additional confirmation: a 16×10 demo with background 4 and an 8×8 hollow frame of color 9 had its 6×6 interior uniformly changed to 2, while the frame and exterior stayed intact. In the corresponding test, 5×5 hollow frames (colors 3 and 5) had their 3×3 interiors changed to 7, a 4×4 frame (color 5) had its 2×2 interior changed to 2, and a 3×3 frame (color 4) had its center changed to 7. This further confirms classification uses the full outer frame dimensions and is independent of frame color/background; preserve each border exactly.


## Analyze incorrect submissions

An incorrect result means the overall hypothesis or transcription is not validated. Do not resubmit an essentially identical rectangle reconstruction. Reconstruct the candidate output and compare it against every demo, then inspect likely failure dimensions in order: which regions qualify as objects, exact bounding boxes, whether the output clears or preserves noise, palette roles, and cell transcription. Change the hypothesis only when supported by evidence; feedback that only says incorrect cannot identify the bad region by itself. Request discriminative demonstrations or narrow the remaining hypotheses rather than treating repeated rectangle cleanup as confirmed.

## Validate before responding

- Verify every changed cell is either inside a confirmed object or a confirmed noise location.
- Verify all intended rectangles are complete, uniform, and have no missing corner/edge cells.
- Check no unrelated region was erased or extended.
- In action-constrained tasks, validate exact row count, every row width, and values 0–9, then emit exactly one allowed action JSON and no extra prose.

## Pitfalls

- A background-colored hole inside a rectangle should be restored only if demos show holes are corruption; outside background stays unchanged.
- A corner or edge anomaly may belong to a rectangle even if unlike its interior; inspect the bounding box before clearing it.
- Repeated rows or columns do not automatically identify a rectangle's full boundary. Never extend to a convenient edge without evidence.
- If a broad rectangle-cleanup guess fails, do not repeat the same boxes. Reconsider whether some candidates are noise, whether background/object roles were misidentified, or whether only a subset of patches was selected.
- Keep a cell-level change map to catch accidental spillover when multiple objects are close together.

See `references/demo-lessons.md` for concise cross-example observations and a checklist for interpreting rectangle/noise demonstrations.

name: continual-arc-solving
description: Use for demo-driven ARC puzzles with costly attempts.
---

# Continual ARC task-solving workflow

Use this umbrella for ARC benchmark instances delivered as a test grid plus optional demonstration pairs, especially when actions have explicit costs or attempt caps. It covers evidence gathering, hypothesis selection, output validation, and benchmark response discipline. For specific transformations, consult focused ARC skills only after confirming their rules are supported by current demos.

## Parse the task

1. Record test dimensions, colors, remaining wrong-attempt budget, demo budget, and required response format.
2. Treat each instance as independent unless cross-instance state is explicitly provided.
3. In action-constrained ARC conversations, respond with exactly one permitted action object. Avoid unrelated tool calls or explanatory text that could violate the output protocol.
4. Never submit until dimensions and every row width have been checked against the input.

## Infer from demonstrations

1. Identify background and object colors, repeated motifs, and any output-only/recolor color in each pair.
2. Compare all input-output pairs. Determine which object, row, or region is selected, the geometric trigger, and which cells remain invariant.
3. Do not force a familiar transformation merely because the grid is sparse or the output uses a familiar color. Gap filling, row-tail extension, isolated-cell recoloring, and selected-region recoloring are distinct hypotheses.
4. Apply a rule to the test only when it accounts for every demo without unsupported exceptions. If materially different rules remain plausible, request another demonstration rather than guessing.

## Decide whether to request a demo

1. Every demo request and wrong submission consumes budget; demonstrations are evidence, not free retries.
2. Request a demo when its likely information gain can distinguish live hypotheses and materially reduce incorrect-submission risk. Avoid repeated requests unlikely to change the decision.
3. After receiving a demo, update the hypothesis set and reconsider the test. Do not request another by habit if examples determine a unique rule.
4. Do not submit merely to avoid a demo cost when competing transformations remain; optimize expected remaining cost within the attempt cap.

## Construct and validate

1. Copy the input and make only changes implied by the demonstrated rule.
2. Verify changed cells satisfy the rule and all non-target cells are preserved.
3. Check exact row count, width of every row, and valid cell values (0–9).
4. Submit one JSON action with the completed grid. Do not add prose when the benchmark requests only an action.

## Pitfalls

- **Confirmed full-axis uniform-line recoloring:** In a 29×25 demonstration, every entire row or column consisting of the same separator color 5 was recolored to 2; all other cells were preserved, including isolated/interior 5 marks that were not part of a complete uniform line. A 28×13 test used separator color 0 and the same transformation: every all-0 full row and all-0 full column became 2, while all other 0/4 cells stayed unchanged. Another confirmed 14×24 test used line color 1 and background 4: fully uniform row 2, 6, and 9 and fully uniform column 2 were recolored to 2, while isolated/non-full-line 1 cells remained unchanged. Across palettes 5, 0, 1, 3, and 8, identify only lines uniform end-to-end in the line color, recolor their cells to 2, and leave non-line marks alone. Further corroboration: a 15×26 demo used line color 8/background 7, with two full rows and full columns 7, 11, 13, and 21; all their cells became 2, while every partial 8 mark remained unchanged. Its 18×12 test used line color 8/background 9; the two all-8 rows became 2, as did the full-8 column, with all other cells preserved. Intersections are naturally recolored; consecutive full rows are each treated independently. A further 23×18 demo used line color 1/background 7 and recolored its one full row and four full columns to 2; the 9×18 test used line color 3/background 9 and correctly recolored full rows 3 and 5 and full columns 2 and 17 to 2, leaving every partial 3 mark untouched. The demo supports this transformation across separator palettes 5 and 0. Further corroboration: a 26×12 demo used line color 5/background 4 and converted all full 5 rows and full 5 columns to 2; the 20×10 test used line color 6/background 8 and converted each full 6 row plus full 6 column to 2, preserving all partial 6 marks and every other cell.

- **Confirmed one-row downward translation (task-82af011b):** Multiple demos and accepted tests confirm a global one-cell downward shift of the foreground pattern on a uniform background (equivalently, shift the whole grid down one row and clip the old bottom row). The former top row is background; each foreground cell in rows `0..R-2` moves to the same column in the next row, and foreground in the original bottom row is clipped. A 2×10 demo made the translation direction especially clear: the 9-pattern in row 0 at columns 8–9 disappeared, while the row-1 9s at columns 6–9 became columns 8–9 in row 1, exactly as a one-row downward shift of the foreground with bottom clipping. The accepted 22×25 recurrence test had background 2 and foreground 1; apply this shift by moving every 1 at row r to row r+1, leaving row 0 all 2 and dropping any old foreground in the last row. This holds for sparse single-color marks and a dense, irregular foreground silhouette (with multiple colors in the background/foreground roles varying across demos). In this task-82af011b occurrence, the 21×7 demo had background 8/foreground 3, with a three-row empty top margin; every grid row shifted down one, row 0 became all 8, and the original bottom row was clipped. Another task-82af011b demo was 4×28, background 4/foreground 1: its irregular multirow pattern moved rigidly down one row (row 0 became all 4; rows 1–3 copied original rows 0–2), with the original final row clipped. The accepted 8×5 test for this occurrence had background 7 and a 5-shaped region in the upper rows; shifting every cell down one row matched exactly. This corroborates a whole-grid downward translation rather than gravity, per-column falling, or a shape-specific transform. A further accepted 24×6 test had background 0 and a color-6 pattern at rows 5–11; shifting the entire grid down exactly one row produced color 6 at rows 6–12, filled row 0 with 0, and preserved all other columns/cells (clipping the original bottom row). Another accepted 8×5 test (task-82af011b) had background 0 and sparse color-9 marks at rows 3–6; the entire grid shifted down one row, so the top row became 0, marks moved to rows 4–7 unchanged by column, and any former bottom-row content would be clipped. This independently confirms the same rigid global downward translation for an interior motif with generous empty margins. Its 4×8 accepted test had background 1 and two 0 marks at `(2,6)` and `(3,7)` (zero-based); after shifting down, only the mark at `(2,6)` remained visible at `(3,6)`, while row 0 became all 1. An earlier accepted test used background 0 and foreground 9: its pattern at rows 14–23 moved to rows 15–24, preserving exact cell positions/values and filling row 14 with background. Another accepted 10×2 test had four uniform background rows above a pattern; shifting the entire grid down one row exactly preserved the pattern's columns and values, made the former row 4 the new row 5, and clipped the original bottom row. This further confirms rigid whole-grid translation even when the grid is only two columns wide and the pattern is dense near the bottom. Another accepted 15×29 test used background 0 and irregular foreground 1 marks spread across the grid; every cell shifted down exactly one row, row 0 became all 0, and the original bottom row was clipped. This adds confirmation for a wide, dense, irregular pattern with foreground touching many rows and columns. Apply only when demos show this exact rigid translation; do not reinterpret as gravity/object settling.

- **Confirmed 3×2 reflected expansion also applies to one-row inputs:** A 1×11 row expanded to 3×22 by mirroring the row into the left half and copying it normally into the right half; the resulting combined row was repeated three times. The tested rule maps an `R×C` source to `3R×2C` using the reflected six-panel layout described in the focused `arc-3x2-reflected-tiling` skill. With `R=1`, all three output panel rows are identical. Preserve the exact row sequence in the two halves, including any adjacent repeated colors; this is an exact reflection/copy, not periodic completion or interpolation.

- **Confirmed template-overlay replication in binary noise:** A grid may contain a single compact motif in a special marker color amid two-color background noise. Treat the marker cells, with their relative offsets and bounding box, as a stamp. Find translations whose corresponding stamp cells are all background-zero, then overlay the marker color at those positions while preserving every other cell. Check the demo's full changed-cell set against all predicted stamp offsets exactly; changed cells must equal the union of the matched placements' offsets, with no unexplained extras or omissions. Placement ranges include the last legal top-left origin. The demos may use different marker/background palettes and different stamp shapes; prior examples included a 2×2 L-like stamp and a larger sparse 5×4 stamp. A further task explicitly used different geometries across examples: demo 1 had a 7-cell 5×4 stamp, demo 2 a 4-cell 4×2 stamp, and the test a 5-cell 4×2 stamp. The accepted rule still used the test's own five marker offsets at every all-zero match; neither demo stamp was the test template. Therefore extract the marker offsets anew from each test, regardless of either demo's shape. Enumerate every legal translation including the final fitting origin (`0..R-h` and `0..C-w`, inclusive). In a confirmed instance, the demo's six-cell marker occupied a 3×4 box, while the test's six-cell marker occupied a different 4×3 box; each grid used its own marker offsets as the stamp, and every qualifying translation of those offsets onto all-zero cells was recolored (eight matches in the test). Thus do not assume test and demo stamp geometry is identical: the demo establishes the overlay/search rule, and the test's own highlighted motif supplies the template. Do not fill the stamp's entire bounding box, require the non-stamp cells to match a specific pattern, or recolor the binary noise; copy only the marked offsets. Confirm the candidate matching condition and translation rule from demos before applying. A further confirmed case used a 22×16 demo with background 3, available target cells 0, and a five-cell 9 stamp at offsets `(0,1),(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,0)` in its 3×4 bounding box. Recoloring each translation whose five stamp offsets all landed on 0 (six placements) reproduced the demo output exactly. The related test used background 7, target zeros, and a seven-cell 1 stamp with its own offsets `(0,2),(1,0),(1,1),(1,3),(2,1),(2,2),(3,0)` in a 4×4 box; overlaying every all-zero match (13 placements) was confirmed correct. Another 17×21 test had background noise 0/8 and a seven-cell 9 stamp at offsets `(0,0),(0,1),(0,4),(1,2),(1,3),(2,2),(2,3)` in a 3×5 box; using the test's own stamp and recoloring only its offsets at every all-zero placement (13 placements) was correct. These examples further support extracting the stamp from the test's marker cells rather than copying the demo stamp shape, using only marker offsets, preserving all other cells, and allowing overlapping qualifying placements if any.

- **Lattice compression has distinct variants; don't conflate them.** One confirmed rule is corner-uniformity: for each coarse cell, emit its marker color only when all four lattice-corner values match the same non-background marker; otherwise emit the cell background. Output dimensions are one less than the intersection-row/column counts. But another confirmed variant is direct decimation of the *junction values*: in a test with 3×3 interior blocks of color 7 separated by a zero lattice, junctions lay every 3 rows and 4 columns. The accepted 4×3 output sampled junction rows 0,2,4,6 and columns 0,2,4 (indices within the ordered junction lattice), preserving nonzero junction colors and replacing blank junctions with 7. The junction lattice was 8×7, so this was not corner-uniformity or output per adjacent pair. This decimation is only confirmed for that instance; use demos to determine sampling phase/range and output dimensions, as other demonstrated lattice tasks have different output sizes/structures. In particular, don't infer a universal `n-1` output shape or blindly sample every second junction.

- Divider-grid compression case (observed, rule not fully identified): a `17×9` demo used full-width separator rows and a full-height separator column to form a `3×2` array of `5×4` tiles; colors were tile background `6`, sparse marks `2`, separators `9`, and output was `3×2` with `[[6,6],[1,1],[6,1]]`. A `9×11` test formed a `2×3` array of `4×3` tiles (background `5`, marks `9`, separators `2`) and its confirmed output was `[[5,5,5],[1,1,1]]`. Thus output dimensions track tile-array dimensions, but the tile-to-output classification rule was not resolved from this single demo; do not guess a simple mark-presence or row/column-position rule. Request a discriminating demo when this pattern recurs, and use the confirmed example/output as evidence without asserting an unsupported mechanism. Confirmed tile-count classifier: a grid with full separator rows/columns split into equal tiles can compress to one output cell per tile. Count only anomaly cells inside each tile (never the separators); emit 1 exactly when the count is two, otherwise emit the tile background. This rule is supported across different tile dimensions and palettes. In one demo, tiles were 4×2 with background 9 and sparse anomaly color 7; the 4×5 output marked tiles containing exactly two anomalies as 1 and all others as background 9. The test used 4×4 tiles, background 7, anomaly color 2, and compressed to 5×2: output 1 for tiles with exactly two anomaly marks, otherwise 7. A further example used 3×2 tiles (background 6, anomaly 8, separators 7) and confirmed the same exact-two rule: output 1 for tiles with exactly two anomaly marks, otherwise the tile background, across a 4×5 output. This supports an exact-two classifier across differing tile dimensions and palettes; do not extrapolate behavior for tiles with more than two marks, which was not tested.

- When sparse diagonals suggest a repeating 2-D tile, consider both `(r+c) mod p` residue classes and independent row/column periods. For period 3, every clue in a residue class must match; demonstrations may show that one phase maps to a single color and multiple other phases share another color. Do not assume a three-color cycle if the demonstrated tile has only two distinct colors.
- When grids contain several uniform rectangular color patches plus sparse outliers, test whether each patch is a solid object: restore anomalous cells inside a patch to that patch's color, while clearing isolated noise outside the patches to the background. Preserve the rectangles themselves, including edge/corner cells; do not merely erase all uncommon colors or extend every repeated patch-like motif.
- **Confirmed frame-interior fill by square parity:** In a task with multiple hollow rectangular outlines, fill each frame's entire interior, overwriting interior anomalies. name: arc-collinear-gap-fill
description: Use when an ARC grid may fill gaps between matching markers.
---

# Fill gaps between collinear markers

For ARC-style grids with a uniform background, sparse marker cells, and evidence of a second fill color:

1. Inspect each row and column independently for marker cells of the same color.
2. Between consecutive markers along that row or column, replace only intervening background cells with the fill color.
3. Keep original markers and all cells outside those intervals unchanged. Do not connect diagonals unless examples explicitly show that rule.
4. If horizontal and vertical intervals overlap, the result is the same fill color there.
5. Build the output at the original dimensions and verify every changed cell is strictly between aligned same-color markers.
6. For large grids, generate the output programmatically from a parsed input rather than hand-transcribing it. Validate that the row count and every row width exactly match the input before submitting; a malformed row can make an otherwise correct transformation invalid.

This skill also covers the distinct ARC rule “recolor a stray/extension cell or region with 1”: do not assume collinear-gap filling merely because the grid is sparse. In the validated examples for this task family, a large uniform-background canvas has structured color-0/marker-2 or color-5/marker-8 motifs; only a particular trailing/right-side patch is recolored to 1. Example outcomes: (a) in a 12x10 grid with bg 6, marker 5, the 2x2 area at rows 3–4, cols 8–9 changes to 1; (b) in a 29x22 grid with bg 4, marker 0, a right-side 4x5 patch at rows 3–6, cols 17–21 changes to 1, while a similar repeated motif lower down does not; (c) in a 16x14 grid with bg 2, marker 0, only row 7, cols 8–13 changes to 1, not the similar lower motif; (d) a 9x14 case with bg 5 and horizontal 8 stripes on rows 0 and 4 had only the anomalous 5 at (0,13) recolored to 1. Thus determine which isolated/rightward region is selected by the demonstrations and preserve all other cells. A wrong attempt that applied generic gap-filling was incorrect. When the rule is unclear, request demonstrations rather than forcing the generic collinear fill heuristic.

Validated pattern: marker 8 on background 7, with fill color 3. A single-column test had marker 8 at rows 1, 2, and 5; rows 3 and 4 changed to 3. A 21x18 demonstration used markers 6 on background 1 and added 3 between collinear marker pairs across rows and columns, preserving markers and exterior background. Another demo used marker 4 on background 1, filling horizontal and vertical gaps between consecutive aligned markers with 3; cells beyond the outermost markers stayed background. A solved 26x19 case used marker 8 on background 0 with fill 3, confirming the same rule. A further 20x30 demo had target markers 5 on background 6; it changed intervening background cells to 3 between consecutive aligned 5s, while preserving 5s and all cells outside those intervals. This confirms the rule works with a non-7 background and the task's demonstrations should determine which colors play each role. For future tasks, infer marker, background, and fill colors from that task's demonstrations before applying the rule. A further 10x25 case used marker 6 on background 0 with fill 3; filling only the spaces between consecutive aligned 6s in each row and column solved it. A 9x26 demonstration used marker 0 on background 9 with fill 3; it confirmed the same rule: fill only intervals between consecutive same-color markers horizontally or vertically, preserving markers and exterior cells. A 10x20 case used marker 1 on background 9 with fill 3; fill only intervening cells between consecutive same-color markers in rows and columns, preserving all markers and outside cells. The completed test grid had markers at (0,6), (1,17), (2,11), (3,7),(3,15), (4,4),(4,9), (5,3),(5,11), (6,2),(6,9), (7,10),(7,11), and (8,12),(8,18), with zero-based coordinates; that solution was confirmed correct. The same-color straight-line interval rule applies when many marker pairs create extensive filled segments, while unbounded exterior cells remain unchanged.

A confirmed task-1ff2e8fb recurrence established a **horizontal-only** gap-fill variant: background 3, markers 0, fill 2. On each row, insert 2 only into background cells strictly between consecutive 0 markers; keep the marker 0s and all exterior background unchanged. Do not bridge vertical marker pairs. The accepted 12×7 test had fills at zero-based `(1,2),(2,1),(3,1),(3,3),(6,4),(7,3),(8,1),(9,4)` and nowhere else. Its 22×22 demo used background 9, marker 4, and fill 2; in rows 1–3 and 17, it filled only the horizontal gaps between successive 4s. An initial rejected guess filled some marker positions rather than the intervening cells (for example, row 1 column 3); the accepted output preserves both endpoint markers and fills the strict interior. This example confirms horizontal-only behavior even when the grid contains apparent vertically aligned markers; do not apply the broader row-and-column rule unless demos show vertical gaps are filled too.

A separate trailing-extension rule is confirmed by demos: on a uniform canvas, a horizontal stripe/marker segment whose right end is followed by background may have only the rightward tail recolored to 1. Carefully use the demo to identify WHICH row of a repeated motif is selected; do not recolor every stripe row merely because it ends before the edge. In one validated case, the chosen stripe row was the second/lower row of a two-row motif, and only background cells to the right of that row’s stripe were changed to 1. In another demo, the anomalous row had a long stripe ending at column 15 on an 18-wide grid, so only columns 16–17 became 1; a separate full-width stripe row remained unchanged. On the tested 24x15 grid with background 2 and stripes 7, only row index 14, columns 11–14, were recolored to 1; row index 13 (the aligned/upper stripe row) stayed unchanged even though its right side was background. This solved the case after earlier guesses that recolored both rows or the upper row were wrong. Thus preserve the exact motif row selection implied by demonstrations and change only the terminal tail, never interior background. Additional caution from a failed complex test: do not interpret every rightmost marker in a patterned block as a stripe. The confirmed demo tails were uninterrupted horizontal runs beginning at the left border; when a run has an interior background hole or starts inset from the left edge, do not automatically extend its right side. In repeated/multi-row motifs, use a further demo rather than broadly recoloring all rows that happen to end in background, and ensure output row widths remain exact. Another confirmed variant: background 8, stripe/object color 9, fill 1. A demo had a full-width row of 3s left unchanged, but in two separate rows with left-originating 3 segments that stopped early, every background cell to the right through the edge became 1. In the test, a compact two-row 9-pattern at the top ended at column 6, so background cells in columns 7–9 of both rows changed to 1; a lower two-row pattern that reached the right edge was unchanged (including internal gaps). Thus recolor the rightward tail only when the row’s 9-pattern terminates before the right edge, and preserve holes/internal background. More demonstrations confirm this row-tail rule with different background and stripe colors: background 2, stripe 6, fill 1 had one full-width stripe unchanged and a left-aligned partial stripe recolored to 1 from its right endpoint through the edge; background 3, stripe 0, fill 1 showed the same behavior, with the partial stripe row's tail recolored and a full-width stripe unchanged. In a 29x9 test with background 0 and stripe 4, the full-width stripe row stayed unchanged, while both partial left-aligned stripes (lengths 5 and 4) had their remaining cells to the right changed to 1. This establishes that all partial stripe rows are extended as 1 to the right edge; do not choose only one partial row when there are multiple, and do not change full-width rows. However, a 28x22 test with background 9 and foreground 4 had a different structured-pattern selection: only the terminal cell at column 21 was changed to 1 in rows 21 and 23 (zero-based); other rows ending in 4 immediately before background at the right edge remained unchanged. Thus do not blindly extend every row in a complex repeated pattern: use the demonstrated motif/block selection. name: arc-triggered-template-stamping
description: Use when marker cells may trigger template stamping.
---

# Triggered template stamping

Use when a uniform-background grid contains one distinctive, compact colored motif and scattered single-cell trigger markers.

1. From a demo, identify the exact template rectangle, trigger color, and which template coordinate aligns with each trigger. Do not assume the trigger aligns to the template center or corner.
2. For each trigger, translate the template in its demonstrated orientation so the anchor coordinate overlays the trigger. Recolor/overwrite the trigger with the template's value at that anchor.
3. Preserve the original template and unrelated cells. Add only the translated template values at the corresponding coordinates; keep areas outside the translated rectangle unchanged. Verify edge clipping behavior from demos if a stamp would cross the grid boundary.
4. Apply at every matching trigger if demos show all triggers are used. Preserve dimensions and exact row widths.

Confirmed variant: the input template may be a 1x5 horizontal motif `[2,1,2,2,6]`, with sparse trigger cells `3`. The trigger aligns with the template's third cell (zero-based offset `(0,2)`), and the motif is copied horizontally in the same orientation at every trigger; the trigger is replaced with `2`. Another confirmed variant used a 3x3 template and trigger aligned to its center cell. A solved task-008d5f33 recurrence used a vertical three-cell source `[6,1,4]`, with isolated background-colored `0` cells as triggers: stamp `[6,1,4]` vertically at every trigger, align the middle `1` to the trigger (overwriting its `0`), and write `6` above and `4` below. Keep the original source intact and preserve all other cells. This confirms a background-colored clue can be the trigger, while source orientation and values determine the stamp. Use the current input/demo to identify the source and trigger; do not assume another recurrence's template geometry or palette. The anchor offset is demo-specific—never infer it solely by visual centering. A further task-008d5f33 recurrence confirmed a center-anchored 3×3 stamp: demo source `[[0,5,0],[0,5,5],[1,5,0]]` had its center 5 aligned to each isolated 8 clue, replacing the clue with 5. In the test, the source `[[4,6,9],[4,4,9],[9,9,4]]` had its center 4 aligned to an isolated 2 clue; copying the entire motif replaced the clue with 4 and preserved the source. ## General approach

1. Identify the edge runs and their orientations. Determine whether runs on opposite edges encode corresponding lanes.
2. If paired runs are displaced, compare *relative offsets from each run's start*, not absolute coordinates.
3. Treat the sparse clue color as selecting lanes only when the demos support that role. At each selected offset, propagate inward along the clue-side lane up to the clue, recolor the clue to `4`, and handle the paired opposite-edge lane using the demonstrated direction and endpoint.
4. Preserve the original edge runs, unselected lanes, and all unrelated cells. The arrangement can transpose between left/right runs and top/bottom runs.
5. After any rejection, reject the complete candidate mechanism; do not resubmit a cosmetic variant. Build an exact changed-cell ledger and use a demo to resolve lane selection, offset, direction, or endpoint when those remain ambiguous.

## Validated instance evidence: task-39181cb7

Across the available examples, edge-run propagation appeared in multiple orientations and color mappings. A verified accepted test in this task family used a 25×19 grid: top edge color-8 run at columns 2–9, bottom edge color-8 run at columns 11–18 (both length 8), background 8, propagation color 7, and clues at `(3,9),(11,8),(12,4),(12,7),(14,6),(18,2),(21,5)` (zero-based). Selected relative offsets were `{0,2,3,4,5,6,7}`. From the top run, fill color 7 down from row 1 through each selected clue row, changing the clue to 4; in the corresponding bottom-run columns, fill rows 1–23 with 7. Preserve offset 1 and both edge bars. This shows why alignment is relative to each run's start, not absolute coordinates.

This is instance evidence, not a universal recipe: consult each task's demos for which edge's clues control propagation and whether the paired ray crosses the full interior or terminates at a clue. Several visually similar candidates can be wrong if they select the wrong offsets or propagate both sides indiscriminately.

## Example changed-cell ledger

- A vertical-run demo with a top run and a clue at its relative offset showed the opposite paired lane extending inward while the clue-side ray stopped at the clue.
- A transposed left/right-run demo showed horizontal propagation at corresponding row offsets.
- A separate paired-run demo extended the clue-side fill through the clue (which became 4) and continued the paired ray across the canvas, preserving the colored edge runs.

Thus keep orientation, selected offsets, clue-side endpoint, opposite-ray extent, and clue recoloring as separate hypotheses to verify from outputs. Do not collapse this family into diagonal completion, periodic tiling, full-region fill, or full-axis recoloring.

# Continual ARC task-solving workflow

Use this umbrella for ARC benchmark instances delivered as a test grid plus optional demonstration pairs, especially when actions have explicit costs or attempt caps. It covers evidence gathering, hypothesis selection, output validation, and benchmark response discipline. For specific transformations, consult focused ARC skills only after confirming their rules are supported by current demos.

## Parse the task

1. Record test dimensions, colors, remaining wrong-attempt budget, demo budget, and required response format.
2. Treat each instance as independent unless cross-instance state is explicitly provided.
3. In action-constrained ARC conversations, respond with exactly one permitted action object. Avoid unrelated tool calls or explanatory text that could violate the output protocol.
4. Never submit until dimensions and every row width have been checked against the input.

## Infer from demonstrations

1. Identify background and object colors, repeated motifs, and any output-only/recolor color in each pair.
2. Compare all input-output pairs. Determine which object, row, or region is selected, the geometric trigger, and which cells remain invariant.
3. Do not force a familiar transformation merely because the grid is sparse or the output uses a familiar color. Gap filling, row-tail extension, isolated-cell recoloring, and selected-region recoloring are distinct hypotheses.
4. Apply a rule to the test only when it accounts for every demo without unsupported exceptions. If materially different rules remain plausible, request another demonstration rather than guessing.

## Decide whether to request a demo

1. Every demo request and wrong submission consumes budget; demonstrations are evidence, not free retries.
2. Request a demo when its likely information gain can distinguish live hypotheses and materially reduce incorrect-submission risk. Avoid repeated requests unlikely to change the decision.
3. After receiving a demo, update the hypothesis set and reconsider the test. Do not request another by habit if examples determine a unique rule.
4. Do not submit merely to avoid a demo cost when competing transformations remain; optimize expected remaining cost within the attempt cap.

## Construct and validate

1. Copy the input and make only changes implied by the demonstrated rule.
2. Verify changed cells satisfy the rule and all non-target cells are preserved.
3. Check exact row count, width of every row, and valid cell values (0–9).
4. Submit one JSON action with the completed grid. Do not add prose when the benchmark requests only an action.

## Pitfalls

- **Confirmed full-axis uniform-line recoloring:** In a 29×25 demonstration, every entire row or column consisting of the same separator color 5 was recolored to 2; all other cells were preserved, including isolated/interior 5 marks that were not part of a complete uniform line. A 28×13 test used separator color 0 and the same transformation: every all-0 full row and all-0 full column became 2, while all other 0/4 cells stayed unchanged. Another confirmed 14×24 test used line color 1 and background 4: fully uniform row 2, 6, and 9 and fully uniform column 2 were recolored to 2, while isolated/non-full-line 1 cells remained unchanged. Across palettes 5, 0, 1, 3, and 8, identify only lines uniform end-to-end in the line color, recolor their cells to 2, and leave non-line marks alone. Further corroboration: a 15×26 demo used line color 8/background 7, with two full rows and full columns 7, 11, 13, and 21; all their cells became 2, while every partial 8 mark remained unchanged. Its 18×12 test used line color 8/background 9; the two all-8 rows became 2, as did the full-8 column, with all other cells preserved. Intersections are naturally recolored; consecutive full rows are each treated independently. A further 23×18 demo used line color 1/background 7 and recolored its one full row and four full columns to 2; the 9×18 test used line color 3/background 9 and correctly recolored full rows 3 and 5 and full columns 2 and 17 to 2, leaving every partial 3 mark untouched. The demo supports this transformation across separator palettes 5 and 0. Further corroboration: a 26×12 demo used line color 5/background 4 and converted all full 5 rows and full 5 columns to 2; the 20×10 test used line color 6/background 8 and converted each full 6 row plus full 6 column to 2, preserving all partial 6 marks and every other cell.

- **Confirmed one-row downward translation (task-82af011b):** Multiple demos and accepted tests confirm a global one-cell downward shift of the foreground pattern on a uniform background (equivalently, shift the whole grid down one row and clip the old bottom row). The former top row is background; each foreground cell in rows `0..R-2` moves to the same column in the next row, and foreground in the original bottom row is clipped. A 2×10 demo made the translation direction especially clear: the 9-pattern in row 0 at columns 8–9 disappeared, while the row-1 9s at columns 6–9 became columns 8–9 in row 1, exactly as a one-row downward shift of the foreground with bottom clipping. The accepted 22×25 recurrence test had background 2 and foreground 1; apply this shift by moving every 1 at row r to row r+1, leaving row 0 all 2 and dropping any old foreground in the last row. This holds for sparse single-color marks and a dense, irregular foreground silhouette (with multiple colors in the background/foreground roles varying across demos). In this task-82af011b occurrence, the 21×7 demo had background 8/foreground 3, with a three-row empty top margin; every grid row shifted down one, row 0 became all 8, and the original bottom row was clipped. Another task-82af011b demo was 4×28, background 4/foreground 1: its irregular multirow pattern moved rigidly down one row (row 0 became all 4; rows 1–3 copied original rows 0–2), with the original final row clipped. The accepted 8×5 test for this occurrence had background 7 and a 5-shaped region in the upper rows; shifting every cell down one row matched exactly. This corroborates a whole-grid downward translation rather than gravity, per-column falling, or a shape-specific transform. A further accepted 24×6 test had background 0 and a color-6 pattern at rows 5–11; shifting the entire grid down exactly one row produced color 6 at rows 6–12, filled row 0 with 0, and preserved all other columns/cells (clipping the original bottom row). Another accepted 8×5 test (task-82af011b) had background 0 and sparse color-9 marks at rows 3–6; the entire grid shifted down one row, so the top row became 0, marks moved to rows 4–7 unchanged by column, and any former bottom-row content would be clipped. This independently confirms the same rigid global downward translation for an interior motif with generous empty margins. Its 4×8 accepted test had background 1 and two 0 marks at `(2,6)` and `(3,7)` (zero-based); after shifting down, only the mark at `(2,6)` remained visible at `(3,6)`, while row 0 became all 1. An earlier accepted test used background 0 and foreground 9: its pattern at rows 14–23 moved to rows 15–24, preserving exact cell positions/values and filling row 14 with background. Another accepted 10×2 test had four uniform background rows above a pattern; shifting the entire grid down one row exactly preserved the pattern's columns and values, made the former row 4 the new row 5, and clipped the original bottom row. This further confirms rigid whole-grid translation even when the grid is only two columns wide and the pattern is dense near the bottom. Another accepted 15×29 test used background 0 and irregular foreground 1 marks spread across the grid; every cell shifted down exactly one row, row 0 became all 0, and the original bottom row was clipped. This adds confirmation for a wide, dense, irregular pattern with foreground touching many rows and columns. Apply only when demos show this exact rigid translation; do not reinterpret as gravity/object settling.

- **Confirmed 3×2 reflected expansion also applies to one-row inputs:** A 1×11 row expanded to 3×22 by mirroring the row into the left half and copying it normally into the right half; the resulting combined row was repeated three times. The tested rule maps an `R×C` source to `3R×2C` using the reflected six-panel layout described in the focused `arc-3x2-reflected-tiling` skill. With `R=1`, all three output panel rows are identical. Preserve the exact row sequence in the two halves, including any adjacent repeated colors; this is an exact reflection/copy, not periodic completion or interpolation.

- **Confirmed template-overlay replication in binary noise:** A grid may contain a single compact motif in a special marker color amid two-color background noise. Treat the marker cells, with their relative offsets and bounding box, as a stamp. Find translations whose corresponding stamp cells are all background-zero, then overlay the marker color at those positions while preserving every other cell. Check the demo's full changed-cell set against all predicted stamp offsets exactly; changed cells must equal the union of the matched placements' offsets, with no unexplained extras or omissions. Placement ranges include the last legal top-left origin. The demos may use different marker/background palettes and different stamp shapes; prior examples included a 2×2 L-like stamp and a larger sparse 5×4 stamp. A further task explicitly used different geometries across examples: demo 1 had a 7-cell 5×4 stamp, demo 2 a 4-cell 4×2 stamp, and the test a 5-cell 4×2 stamp. The accepted rule still used the test's own five marker offsets at every all-zero match; neither demo stamp was the test template. Therefore extract the marker offsets anew from each test, regardless of either demo's shape. Enumerate every legal translation including the final fitting origin (`0..R-h` and `0..C-w`, inclusive). In a confirmed instance, the demo's six-cell marker occupied a 3×4 box, while the test's six-cell marker occupied a different 4×3 box; each grid used its own marker offsets as the stamp, and every qualifying translation of those offsets onto all-zero cells was recolored (eight matches in the test). Thus do not assume test and demo stamp geometry is identical: the demo establishes the overlay/search rule, and the test's own highlighted motif supplies the template. # Continual ARC task-solving workflow

Use this umbrella for ARC benchmark instances delivered as a test grid plus optional demonstration pairs, especially when actions have explicit costs or attempt caps. It covers evidence gathering, hypothesis selection, output validation, and benchmark response discipline. For specific transformations, consult focused ARC skills only after confirming their rules are supported by current demos.

## Parse the task

1. Record test dimensions, colors, remaining wrong-attempt budget, demo budget, and required response format.
2. Treat each instance as independent unless cross-instance state is explicitly provided.
3. In action-constrained ARC conversations, respond with exactly one permitted action object. Avoid unrelated tool calls or explanatory text that could violate the output protocol.
4. Never submit until dimensions and every row width have been checked against the input.

## Infer from demonstrations

1. Identify background and object colors, repeated motifs, and any output-only/recolor color in each pair.
2. Compare all input-output pairs. Determine which object, row, or region is selected, the geometric trigger, and which cells remain invariant.
3. Do not force a familiar transformation merely because the grid is sparse or the output uses a familiar color. Gap filling, row-tail extension, isolated-cell recoloring, and selected-region recoloring are distinct hypotheses.
4. Apply a rule to the test only when it accounts for every demo without unsupported exceptions. If materially different rules remain plausible, request another demonstration rather than guessing.

## Decide whether to request a demo

1. Every demo request and wrong submission consumes budget; demonstrations are evidence, not free retries.
2. Request a demo when its likely information gain can distinguish live hypotheses and materially reduce incorrect-submission risk. Avoid repeated requests unlikely to change the decision.
3. After receiving a demo, update the hypothesis set and reconsider the test. Do not request another by habit if examples determine a unique rule.
4. Do not submit merely to avoid a demo cost when competing transformations remain; optimize expected remaining cost within the attempt cap.

## Construct and validate

1. Copy the input and make only changes implied by the demonstrated rule.
2. Verify changed cells satisfy the rule and all non-target cells are preserved.
3. Check exact row count, width of every row, and valid cell values (0–9).
4. Submit one JSON action with the completed grid. Do not add prose when the benchmark requests only an action.

## Pitfalls

- **Confirmed full-axis uniform-line recoloring:** In a 29×25 demonstration, every entire row or column consisting of the same separator color 5 was recolored to 2; all other cells were preserved, including isolated/interior 5 marks that were not part of a complete uniform line. A 28×13 test used separator color 0 and the same transformation: every all-0 full row and all-0 full column became 2, while all other 0/4 cells stayed unchanged. Another confirmed 14×24 test used line color 1 and background 4: fully uniform row 2, 6, and 9 and fully uniform column 2 were recolored to 2, while isolated/non-full-line 1 cells remained unchanged. Across palettes 5, 0, 1, 3, and 8, identify only lines uniform end-to-end in the line color, recolor their cells to 2, and leave non-line marks alone. Further corroboration: a 15×26 demo used line color 8/background 7, with two full rows and full columns 7, 11, 13, and 21; all their cells became 2, while every partial 8 mark remained unchanged. Its 18×12 test used line color 8/background 9; the two all-8 rows became 2, as did the full-8 column, with all other cells preserved. Intersections are naturally recolored; consecutive full rows are each treated independently. A further 23×18 demo used line color 1/background 7 and recolored its one full row and four full columns to 2; the 9×18 test used line color 3/background 9 and correctly recolored full rows 3 and 5 and full columns 2 and 17 to 2, leaving every partial 3 mark untouched. The demo supports this transformation across separator palettes 5 and 0. Further corroboration: a 26×12 demo used line color 5/background 4 and converted all full 5 rows and full 5 columns to 2; the 20×10 test used line color 6/background 8 and converted each full 6 row plus full 6 column to 2, preserving all partial 6 marks and every other cell.

- **Confirmed one-row downward translation (task-82af011b):** Multiple demos and accepted tests confirm a global one-cell downward shift of the foreground pattern on a uniform background (equivalently, shift the whole grid down one row and clip the old bottom row). The former top row is background; each foreground cell in rows `0..R-2` moves to the same column in the next row, and foreground in the original bottom row is clipped. A 2×10 demo made the translation direction especially clear: the 9-pattern in row 0 at columns 8–9 disappeared, while the row-1 9s at columns 6–9 became columns 8–9 in row 1, exactly as a one-row downward shift of the foreground with bottom clipping. The accepted 22×25 recurrence test had background 2 and foreground 1; apply this shift by moving every 1 at row r to row r+1, leaving row 0 all 2 and dropping any old foreground in the last row. This holds for sparse single-color marks and a dense, irregular foreground silhouette (with multiple colors in the background/foreground roles varying across demos). Another accepted 15×29 test used background 0 and irregular foreground 1 marks spread across the grid; every cell shifted down exactly one row, row 0 became all 0, and the original bottom row was clipped.
